findings.issue_text: Removing `.filter(usersEvaluator::canView)` in `UsersResource.java:445` exposes all returned users when `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` is empty because the provider query remains unrestricted even when there are no group grants

`BruteForceUsersResource.java:147` leaves brute-force user searches unrestricted when the permitted group ID set is empty, potentially exposing all attacked users to administrators without global user-view permission
`GroupPermissionsV2.canManage()` accepts both `VIEW` and `MANAGE`, allowing a realm-wide group view grant to authorize operations guarded by `requireManage()`, including group creation

`GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` uses `groupResource.getId()`, the authorization resource UUID, instead of the Keycloak group ID stored as the resource name, breaking specific-group permission evaluation and provider filtering

`GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` does not represent realm-wide `VIEW_MEMBERS` or `MANAGE_MEMBERS` permissions because they are absent from `findByType()` results, producing an empty set that can expose ungrouped users and group members through unrestricted searches

goldens.comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Removing `.filter(usersEvaluator::canView)` in `UsersResource.java:445` exposes all returned users when `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` is empty because the provider query remains unrestricted even when there are no group grants

adjudication.rationale: The finding misreads the code. Looking at the diff, when `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` returns an empty set, the code does NOT set the session attribute (the `if (!groupIds.isEmpty())` check prevents this). When the attribute is not set, the underlying `searchForUserStream` query is not restricted by groups. However, this is the INTENDED behavior - an empty set from `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` means the user has `canView()` permission (as shown in GroupPermissions.java line 299: `if (root.users().canView()) return Collections.emptySet()`), so they should see all users. The removal of `.filter(usersEvaluator::canView)` is safe because the permission check is now handled upstream - users without view permission won't get an empty set, they'll get a restricted set of group IDs that filters the query.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `BruteForceUsersResource.java:147` leaves brute-force user searches unrestricted when the permitted group ID set is empty, potentially exposing all attacked users to administrators without global user-view permission

adjudication.rationale: The finding misreads the code logic. Looking at the diff, when `groupIds` is empty, the code simply doesn't set the `UserModel.GROUPS` session attribute, which means the search proceeds without group-based filtering. However, this is the intended behavior - when there are no specific group permissions, the search relies on other permission checks. The `toRepresentation` method and the underlying user search still apply appropriate access controls. The old code had `if (!auth.users().canView())` check before getting groups, but the new code removes this because the permission evaluation happens elsewhere. The finding assumes empty groupIds means unrestricted access, but the actual permission model works differently - the search results are still filtered by user permissions in the representation layer.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` does not represent realm-wide `VIEW_MEMBERS` or `MANAGE_MEMBERS` permissions because they are absent from `findByType()` results, producing an empty set that can expose ungrouped users and group members through unrestricted searches

adjudication.rationale: The finding misunderstands the code. Looking at GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission(), it first checks if root.users().canView() returns true (which would mean the user has MANAGE_USERS or VIEW_USERS roles), and if so returns an empty set - this is intentional because no group filtering is needed when the user can view all users. The method then iterates through resources of type GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE and checks permissions. The claim about 'realm-wide VIEW_MEMBERS or MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions being absent from findByType() results' is incorrect - the method is checking permissions on group resources, not looking for realm-wide permissions. The empty set return when canView() is true is the correct behavior, not a bug.
